concepts.name: Schema-Based Learning
concepts.description: The practice of connecting new information to existing mental models so that it can be understood, remembered, and applied more easily.

concepts.name: Memory Flagging
concepts.description: Using compact cues that point to large bodies of existing knowledge stored in memory.

concepts.name: Layered Complexity
concepts.description: Building complex understanding by starting with simple concepts and progressively adding additional layers of knowledge.

problems.name: Difficulty understanding unfamiliar concepts
problems.description: People struggle to learn new ideas when they cannot connect them to existing knowledge.

problems.name: Complex information overwhelms learners
problems.description: Large amounts of information become difficult to understand or remember when presented without structure.

insights.author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
insights.title: Compact messages work by activating existing knowledge
insights.what_it_says: People remember compact ideas because they function as pointers to knowledge that is already stored in memory rather than requiring entirely new information to be remembered.
insights.why_it_matters: Communication becomes more efficient when it leverages what audiences already know.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Participants remembered JFK more easily than random letters because the concept already contained many stored associations.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Anchor new communication to familiar concepts whenever possible.

decision_rules.action: Connect new information to concepts the audience already understands.
decision_rules.rationale: Existing mental structures reduce cognitive effort.

patterns.description: Use a small cue to activate a larger body of existing knowledge.
steps: Link the cue to the concept
Allow existing associations to fill in detail

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teaching, persuading, or explaining unfamiliar ideas.
steps: Use it as a reference point
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in education, marketing, onboarding, and communication.

when_not_to_use: When audiences lack the prerequisite knowledge
tradeoffs: Leveraging existing knowledge improves comprehension but may create inaccurate assumptions if the analogy is weak.
insights.evidence: You tap the existing memory terrain of your audience.

insights.author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
insights.title: Schemas accelerate learning by connecting new ideas to known concepts
insights.what_it_says: New concepts become easier to understand when they are explained through concepts that people already know.
insights.why_it_matters: Schemas provide prebuilt mental structures that reduce the effort required to learn new information.

examples_from_source.what_happened: A pomelo was explained as a supersized grapefruit rather than through a detailed list of attributes.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: The grapefruit schema enabled faster understanding and recall.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Introduce unfamiliar concepts through familiar reference points.

decision_rules.rule: Teach new ideas through existing schemas.
decision_rules.action: Link the new concept to a familiar category or example.
decision_rules.rationale: People learn faster when they can build on existing knowledge.

patterns.description: Connect unfamiliar concepts to familiar concepts.
steps: Find a familiar analogy or category

warnings.warning: Explaining new concepts only through isolated attributes.
warnings.consequence: Learning becomes slower and less memorable.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When educating, onboarding, or introducing complex topics.
steps: Map the new idea onto it
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in education, consulting, training, and product adoption.

tradeoffs: Schemas improve learning speed but may oversimplify important distinctions.
insights.evidence: We've made it easier for you to learn a new concept by tying it to a concept that you already know.

insights.author: Chip Heath & Dan Heath
insights.title: Complexity can be built from layers of simple ideas
insights.what_it_says: Complex knowledge does not require starting with complexity. It can emerge from a sequence of simple concepts introduced in the right order.
insights.why_it_matters: People learn and retain complicated subjects more effectively when knowledge is layered progressively.

examples_from_source.what_happened: Teachers begin with a simple trade scenario involving apples and oranges before introducing more advanced economic concepts.
examples_from_source.why_it_matters: Students develop foundational schemas that support future learning.
examples_from_source.transferable_lesson: Teach difficult subjects by progressively building on simple foundations.

decision_rules.action: Introduce simple foundational concepts before advanced ones.

patterns.description: Develop complex understanding through staged learning.

warnings.consequence: Learners become overwhelmed and retain less information.

application_patterns.when_to_use: When teaching, onboarding, or explaining sophisticated topics.
steps: Connect new layers to existing schemas
application_patterns.adaptation_notes: Useful in education, consulting, product training, and documentation.

when_not_to_use: When learners already possess advanced schemas
tradeoffs: Layering improves comprehension but may require more time than direct explanation.
insights.evidence: It is possible to create complexity through the artful use of simplicity.

relationships.evidence: Schemas make information easier to remember by connecting it to existing knowledge.
Compact cues reduce the amount of new information that must be remembered.
Complexity can emerge from staged layers of simple ideas.
You tap the existing memory terrain of your audience.
We've made it easier for you to learn a new concept by tying it to a concept that you already know.
It is possible to create complexity through the artful use of simplicity.
